article_title: Partnerships that Work: Tapping Research to Address Learner Variability in Young Readers
citation: Tare, M., Nobles, S., & Xiao, W. (2018). Partnerships that work: Tapping research to address learner variability in young readers. Washington, DC: Digital Promise Global. https://www.digitalpromise.org/
title: LPS-edtech developer partnership process for research-based product improvement
description: LPS partnerships with developers follow a collaborative process: explore the mission and goals of the existing product; review product features against LPS to identify supports for learner variability; create an assessment report highlighting key potential improvements; co-create a development plan and timeline; implement product features; conduct research to assess how new features support more learner variability; and cross-promote to advance research-based products. Features are categorized into short-, mid-, and long-term phases of development aligned with the partner's roadmap.
requirements: Partner organizations committed to reaching learners from a variety of backgrounds and with varying needs
constraints: The first set of partnerships specifically sought products focused on readers in pre-kindergarten through third grade to leverage the Reading PK-3 model
target_learners: Pre-K through third grade readers with varying needs
target_learning_goals: Reading achievement supported by evidence-based product features
examples: The ReadWorks partnership produced a draft assessment report finalized jointly, with features phased into the product roadmap
key_sources: Tare, M., Nobles, S., & Xiao, W. (2018). Partnerships that work: Tapping research to address learner variability in young readers. Washington, DC: Digital Promise Global. https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/e59c6e47-4209-4187-a0ef-b8da08283ec6

article_title: To Grade or Not To Grade? Demystifying a Centuries-Old Debate
citation: Nicolas Hübner, Juliane Rutsch, Ann-Kathrin Schnelle, Mia Herkommer, Evelin Ruth-Herbein, Benjamin Fauth. (2026). To Grade or Not To Grade? Demystifying a Centuries-Old Debate. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10156-1
title: LPF school trial: grade abolishment with standards-based competency grids, learning-development meetings, and formative feedback
description: The Learning-enhanced Performance Feedback (LPF) school trial was a quasi-experimental intervention in 35 Baden-Württemberg elementary schools beginning in the 2022/2023 school year, compared with 40 control schools. Trial schools abolished written grades and report cards and instead gave "standards-based competency grids" on a 4-point scale from "You still need to work on this" to "You are an expert", at least two oral learning-development meetings per school year, and formative assessment and feedback practices integrated throughout instruction. The grids share many similarities with standards-based grading systems as defined by Welsh et al. (2013) and Guskey and Bailey (2001).
requirements: Trial schools were required to eliminate written grades from Grade 2 onward; implementation was evaluated on behalf of the Ministry of Education and Cultural Affairs
constraints: The trial was implemented with minimal requirements: teachers received no comprehensive professional development and no detailed guidance on formative assessment or feedback practices; standardization of features decreased from the first to the third feature
examples: Competency grids covered predefined areas in German, mathematics, and social studies (e.g., "You read texts fluently", "You can measure sizes") plus behavior, work attitude, and learning process
key_sources: Nicolas Hübner, Juliane Rutsch, Ann-Kathrin Schnelle, Mia Herkommer, Evelin Ruth-Herbein, Benjamin Fauth. (2026). To Grade or Not To Grade? Demystifying a Centuries-Old Debate. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10156-1

article_title: Feuerstein's Mediated Learning Experience as a Vehicle for Enhancing Cognitive Functioning of Remedial School Learners in South Africa
citation: Seabi, J. (2012). Feuerstein's mediated learning experience as a vehicle for enhancing cognitive functioning of remedial school learners in South Africa. Australian Journal of Educational & Developmental Psychology, 12, 35-45. http://www.newcastle.edu.au/journal/ajedp/
title: LPAD Set Variations B-8 to B-12 mediation tasks with the Raven's Coloured Progressive Matrices
description: The study used two instruments from the Learning Potential Assessment Device. The LPAD Set Variations B-8 to B-12 consist of sets of six variations on five Raven's Coloured Progressive Matrices items and were selected because "they permit the examiner to access and to modify the area of abstract thinking, and also represent tasks that under normal circumstances are rarely offered to the low-functioning individual." The RCPM, a nonverbal problem-solving test with sets A, AB and B scored 0 to 36, served as the pre- and post-measure (sets A and AB, scores 0 to 24), with set B used for mediation. Both measure forming comparisons, reasoning by analogy and organising spatial perceptions.
requirements: Standard administration of the RCPM in group setting for pre- and post-test phases
Examiner training in LPAD mediation procedures
constraints: The RCPM has been standardized only in the United Kingdom, the United States of America and Germany, though South African studies support it as a measure of intellectual functioning
target_learners: Low-functioning learners and learners with learning difficulties
target_learning_goals: Abstract thinking, analogical reasoning, comparison-forming and spatial organisation
examples: Problems A and AB of the RCPM were used as pre-post measurements while set B served as the mediation task
key_sources: Seabi, J. (2012). Feuerstein's mediated learning experience as a vehicle for enhancing cognitive functioning of remedial school learners in South Africa. Australian Journal of Educational & Developmental Psychology, 12, 35-45. http://www.newcastle.edu.au/journal/ajedp/

article_title: Computer model for the cardiovascular system: development of an e-learning tool for teaching of medical students.
citation: Warriner DR, Bayley M, Shi Y, Lawford PV, Narracott A, Fenner J. (2017). Computer model for the cardiovascular system: development of an e-learning tool for teaching of medical students. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-017-1058-1
title: Interactive e-learning environment embedding a lumped-parameter cardiovascular model with virtual clinical cases
description: The e-learning environment (ELE) was built in Microsoft Powerpoint, published as a PDF and hosted on the Sheffield Minerva managed learning environment. It combined physiology modules, three pathology areas with interactive pre-computed lumped-parameter model results, and "Three virtual cases ... developed for each pathology to map the model information and help the students place the physiology and model results in clinical context", with built-in questions on diagnosis, treatment, pathophysiology and severity. Outputs were pre-computed rather than solved in real time.
requirements: Requires access via a web-based learning environment (Minerva) and pre-computed model outputs so students need not solve the model in real time
constraints: Students were restricted to a two-week access period and the software was not downloadable; final iteration contained over 200 pages
Results pre-computed, so users could not choose their own combinations of resistance, compliance and cardiac performance
target_learners: undergraduate medical students at all stages of training
target_learning_goals: understanding cardiovascular physiology and pathophysiology (hypertension, heart failure, haemorrhagic shock) in a clinical context
examples: Mild, moderate and severe hypertension were simulated by gradually increasing systemic resistance R, with outputs displayed as pressure traces and a left ventricle pressure-volume loop
key_sources: Warriner DR, Bayley M, Shi Y, Lawford PV, Narracott A, Fenner J. (2017). Computer model for the cardiovascular system: development of an e-learning tool for teaching of medical students. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-017-1058-1

article_title: Computer model for the cardiovascular system: development of an e-learning tool for teaching of medical students.
citation: Warriner DR, Bayley M, Shi Y, Lawford PV, Narracott A, Fenner J. (2017). Computer model for the cardiovascular system: development of an e-learning tool for teaching of medical students. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-017-1058-1
title: E-learning environment structured as physiology modules plus pathology areas with model results and virtual cases
description: The environment's instructional design combined general and topic-specific components: "The environment comprised a general introduction, modules on basic cardiovascular physiology and the three areas of pathology sub-divided into aetiology, epidemiology, pathophysiology, treatments, interactive model results and virtual clinical cases." Questions were embedded in the text at two levels — on model parameters (e.g. how to model hypertension with the LPM) and on the disease itself (e.g. how a heart failure patient would be treated) — with sequential Back/Proceed navigation and a jump navigation tab.
requirements: Embeds assessment questions within the content so the environment includes both interactive and assessment elements
constraints: Maintaining a structured design became challenging in the final iteration, which contained over 200 pages, though users were not required to interact with each page sequentially
target_learning_goals: cardiovascular physiology and pathophysiology knowledge; disease classification and severity grading
examples: A virtual hypertension case presented history, examination, past history and investigation outcomes followed by a choice of four questions with click-revealed answers
key_sources: Warriner DR, Bayley M, Shi Y, Lawford PV, Narracott A, Fenner J. (2017). Computer model for the cardiovascular system: development of an e-learning tool for teaching of medical students. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-017-1058-1

article_title: Towards Scalable Adaptive Learning with Graph Neural Networks and Reinforcement Learning
citation: Jean Vassoyan, Jill-Jênn Vie, Pirmin Lemberger. (2023). Towards Scalable Adaptive Learning with Graph Neural Networks and Reinforcement Learning. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.06398
title: Learning path personalization formalized as a model-free reinforcement learning problem (POMDP) with a three-valued feedback signal as reward
description: The paper formalizes learning path personalization as a partially observable Markov decision process in which the agent is the recommender system and each episode is a learning path of equal length. The learner's knowledge state is unobserved; observations are pairs of recommended document and learner feedback (f<, f>, or f◦). The reward is defined as R(st, at) = 1{ft=f◦}, so "only feedback f◦ corresponds to an eﬀective learning gain". Unlike most prior RL approaches, the formulation is model-free, avoiding overfitting to a predefined student model.
requirements: A feedback signal providing information about user understanding of each resource, assumed perfectly accurate in this study
Resources that are purely textual, self-contained, and of equivalent educational value
constraints: Assumes short learning paths (~1 hour) so learning from previous resources is still in working memory
Assumes no learner interaction with the external world
Assumes each feedback is perfectly accurate, which the authors note is incorrect in most cases
target_learners: Learners on e-learning platforms following short (~1 hour) learning paths
target_learning_goals: Maximizing overall learning gains through personalized sequencing of educational resources
examples: The paper states: "the agent is the recommender system, the environment is the population P of students and each episode is a learning path"
key_sources: Jean Vassoyan, Jill-Jênn Vie, Pirmin Lemberger. (2023). Towards Scalable Adaptive Learning with Graph Neural Networks and Reinforcement Learning. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.06398

article_title: The Impact of Live Polling Quizzes on Student Engagement and Performance in Computer Science Lectures
citation: Xingyu Zhao. (2023). The Impact of Live Polling Quizzes on Student Engagement and Performance in Computer Science Lectures. arXiv preprint arXiv:2309.12335. https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.12335
title: LPQ lecture practice: pre-study videos with unanswered quizzes plus 2-3 in-lecture polls every 15-20 minutes with live explanations
description: This lesson-level practice sends students pre-recorded videos and slides with quizzes (without answers) before each lecture for pre-study, then, as the article reports, "During the lectures, 2-3 LPQs were conducted every 15-20 minutes followed by live explanations and discussions of the answers". The LPQ questions are fact-based and formally defined with clear answers, rather than open-ended or opinion-based.
requirements: A web-based live polling tool and devices for students to respond during lectures
Pre-recorded videos and slides with the quizzes distributed before each lecture for pre-study
constraints: Only one polling software (itempool.com) was studied
Questions were fact-based with clear answers rather than open-ended or opinion-based
target_learning_goals: checking understanding of factual lecture content
examples: The practice ran in a 12-week module with 3 lectures per week for 70 final-year CS students, and the survey was distributed after the mid-term once students had sufficient experience of learning with LPQs.
key_sources: Xingyu Zhao. (2023). The Impact of Live Polling Quizzes on Student Engagement and Performance in Computer Science Lectures. arXiv preprint arXiv:2309.12335. https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.12335

article_title: Validating Light Phenomena Conceptual Assessment Through The Lens of CTT and IRT Frameworks
citation: Purwoko Haryadi Santoso, Edi Istiyono, Haryanto, Heri Retnawati. (2023). Validating Light Phenomena Conceptual Assessment Through The Lens of CTT and IRT Framework. https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-sa/4.0/
title: Light Phenomena Conceptual Assessment (LPCA)
description: The LPCA is a 30-item multiple-choice conceptual inventory of light phenomena, each item with "a correct answer and 3 distractors", designed to probe secondary school through undergraduate physics students' conceptual understanding. It covers constructs including seeing, eclipses, reflection, refraction, scattering, spectroscopy, wave propagation and the photoelectric effect (Table 1). This study validated its psychometric properties using CTT and IRT on pretest data from 283 Rwandan secondary school students.
requirements: Administered as a 40-minute sit; content validity examined by students and faculty members prior to large-scale implementation
constraints: The article reports low reliability (alpha = 0.373), so per Doran (1980) it is more appropriate only for group averages or surveys
Some items (e.g., 18 and 28) have low discriminating power and remain open for further development
examples: Administered to 283 secondary school students at pretest and 278 at posttest across eight Rwandan secondary schools in the source dataset
key_sources: Purwoko Haryadi Santoso, Edi Istiyono, Haryanto, Heri Retnawati. (2023). Validating Light Phenomena Conceptual Assessment Through The Lens of CTT and IRT Framework. https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-sa/4.0/

article_title: Learning with Digital Agents: An Analysis based on the Activity Theory
citation: Mateusz Dolata, Dzmitry Katsiuba, Natalie Wellnhammer, and Gerhard Schwabe (2023) Learning with Digital Agents: An Analysis based on the Activity Theory, Journal of Management Information Systems, 40:1, 56-95, https://doi.org/10.1080/07421222.2023.2172775
title: LPAM: a model of learning with a pedagogical agent as two interdependent activity systems
description: LPAM models learning with a pedagogical agent (LPA) as an ensemble of two interdependent activity systems grounded in Engeström's activity theory: the learner's activity system (LPAM-LAS), whose subject is the learner and whose object is the learning task, and the pedagogical agent's activity system (LPAM-PAAS), 'as perceived by the learner', whose object is the learner's competency. The systems share a collective object — the learner's competency gaps — and outcomes including the completed learning task and new competency. The article uses LPAM to classify design aspects from a systematic review of pedagogical-agent studies and to derive design guidance.
requirements: The model addresses the single-learner scenario interacting with one pedagogical agent, which the authors call the simplest and best-researched application
constraints: The manuscript focuses on the single-learner scenario; only few studies attend to interaction between a PA and multiple learners
LPAM-PAAS is a system perceived by the learner, not a system found in the external world
target_learners: single learners across primary school, secondary school, higher education, and adult/professional contexts
target_learning_goals: acquisition of knowledge and skills needed to complete a learning task, closing competency gaps
examples: The review classifies manipulated design aspects of pedagogical agents (e.g., roles, interaction configurations, contributions) under the LPAM components subject, object, tools, community, rules, and division of labor
key_sources: Mateusz Dolata, Dzmitry Katsiuba, Natalie Wellnhammer, and Gerhard Schwabe (2023) Learning with Digital Agents: An Analysis based on the Activity Theory, Journal of Management Information Systems, 40:1, 56-95, https://doi.org/10.1080/07421222.2023.2172775
